questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — feed and notifications fan-out (javabootcamp System Design, guide astraupskill/03-SYSTEM-DESIGN.md §4.3; blocks from modules 09, 11 and 12). Requirements: users follow others; a user's home feed shows recent posts from people they follow; followers get notified; feed reads far outnumber posts; a few seconds of delay is fine; celebrity accounts have millions of followers. Write your design before you look: sizing, data model and ids, partitioning, the cache layer, failure modes and consistency, and the trade-off you would defend. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70 % with every [w3] hit).

keyPoints.text: [w2] Sizing is driven by the read/write skew and the follower distribution: reads dominate, and one celebrity post multiplied by millions of followers is the number that shapes the write path.
[w2] Posts carry a sortable, time-ordered id (snowflake-style), which gives feed order without a central clock.
[w3] Saving the post and announcing it cannot drift apart: no dual write; the post and its event go through a transactional outbox and a relay.
keyPoints.quote: "Save the order, then publish OrderPlaced" loses the event if the process dies in between

keyPoints.text: [w3] One 'posted' topic with independent consumers (feed fan-out worker, notification worker, indexers), each at-least-once with dedupe because duplicates will arrive.
[w2] Feeds are cached per-user lists, partitioned by user id.
[w2] Failing notifications retry with backoff and land in a dead-letter queue after N attempts; consistency is eventual, since seconds of delay are acceptable.
keyPoints.quote: after N attempts to a **dead-letter queue** for a human to inspect and redrive

keyPoints.text: [w3] Fan-out decided: push to every follower makes reads trivial and celebrity writes enormous, pull makes reads expensive; the hybrid pushes for normal accounts, pulls for celebrities and merges at read time.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the same feed at 10x the traffic (several celebrities posting at once), or with the push/email provider down. What breaks first, and what in your design already prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The fan-out queue spikes; an unbounded queue only postpones the failure to an out-of-memory crash, so it is bounded and producers are slowed (backpressure).
keyPoints.quote: the outage just arrives later, as an OOM

keyPoints.text: [w3] Redelivery is normal: a consumer cannot know whether its ack was lost, so the same post event arrives twice and must not double-insert feed entries or double-notify.
keyPoints.quote: A network can't tell "the consumer crashed before acking" from "the ack got lost"

keyPoints.text: [w2] With the provider down, a message that always fails must not block the others: it moves to a dead-letter queue, and somebody owns reading that queue.
[w2] Bulk fan-out must not delay 'your friend replied': priority scheduling, with the known catch that low priority can starve.
[w2] Notification storms are batched and rate-limited per recipient ('someone and 40 others liked your post').
[w1] Adding partitions to a live topic reshuffles keys and breaks per-key order, so partition count is planned ahead of the spike.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your feed choices against the alternatives the guide names. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Work placement table: fan-out on write buys fast reads at the price of write amplification; fan-out on read buys cheap writes at the price of slow reads; the read-heavy requirement plus celebrities decides the split.

[w3] 'Exactly once' is not offered: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing is what looks exactly-once from outside, and the answer names where the dedupe state lives and how long it is kept.
[w2] Outbox vs dual write: the outbox costs a relay process and at-least-once delivery, accepted because a lost or phantom 'posted' event is worse.
[w2] Asynchronous over synchronous processing: a queue buys decoupling and resilience and costs immediacy, which the few-seconds tolerance allows.
[w1] Feed read models as projections of an event log are rebuildable, at the cost of schema evolution and replay time.
